_about: Shared by every industry: the close sequence, the objection buttons, and the Go deeper panel. An industry file can override any node or objection by using the same id. Paths like "@quick" point at that industry's anchors.

Your terms: Where every job is, from lead to paid.
How long jobs take start to finish (e.g. "signing to PTO averages 70 days").
The stage where jobs pile up.
Accounts receivable: money owed to them, and how old it is.
Percent of quotes that become jobs.
What each job actually cost vs. what they charged.
Info passing between people (field to office). Where things get lost.
Tip: Ask: "What do you mean by a redline?" Asking builds trust. Faking it loses it.

story_opener.question: Story opener: your background, then the free offer
say: Hi, is this {{contact|the owner}}?
Hey, this is {{me}}. Quick cold call.
I specialize in fixing operational bottlenecks for {{trade}}, specifically how field communication and scheduling quietly eat into your margins.

Building the operations side for a solar and electrical contractor showed me most {{trade}} run on chaos. Not because anyone's doing it wrong. The work just moves faster than anyone can write it down.
{{hook}}
So I'm running a free 20-minute {{offerName}} for local {{trade}}. Ten sharp questions about how a job moves, and before we hang up you'll know {{offerGoal}}.
{{offerWhy}}
Does that sound like your shop, or are you running pretty tight?
story_opener.why: The offer is built with Hormozi's MAGIC formula: a reason to act now (free, before the season turns), the avatar (local owners in their trade), the goal (see where jobs and money get stuck), a time box (20 minutes, answer before you hang up) and a container (the Ops Sweep). You lead as the expert running a diagnostic, not a student asking for a favor.. End on a question so they talk next.

answers.label: "What is it exactly? What's the catch?"
Wrong person: get a name and time
Voicemail: hang up, try again in 2 days

story_dig.question: Where does the chaos show up most?
story_dig.say: Ha, you're not alone. Where does it show up most for you right now?
story_dig.why: One question, then let them talk. If they go on about it, open Go deeper. Write their exact words in Notes, because you'll use them at the visit.

answers.label: Quiet or unsure: make a guess

story_tight.question: "We're pretty tight": get curious
story_tight.say: Love that, it's rare. Mind if I ask how you keep it that way? I'm genuinely curious.
story_tight.why: Don't argue. Tight shops love explaining their system, and the gaps show up while they talk.

story_explain.question: Explain the {{offerName}}: no catch
say: No catch. Twenty minutes on the phone. I walk through how a job moves from the first call to the final payment, and I'm listening for where it stalls.
Before we hang up, I tell you straight where your top leaks are and roughly what they're costing you.
If one of them is big, the next step is my paid Field Efficiency Audit. I'll bring it up once. You decide.
story_explain.why: Saying the paid part out loud is what makes the free part believable.

story_book.question: Book the {{offerName}}
say: That's exactly the kind of thing the {{offerName}} finds.
Got 20 minutes right now? Or let's put it on the calendar.
story_book.why: Offer to run it now first: the sweep IS the discovery, and it flows straight into the audit close. If now's bad, book an exact time. Never leave it at 'sometime'.

answers.label: Real pain, wants help now: offer the audit

close_sweep.question: Book the {{offerName}}
say: Great. What's better, tomorrow morning or later this week?
Twenty minutes, by phone. Have whoever knows the jobs best close by.
Send me a text with the best email and I'll send the invite.
close_sweep.why: Book an exact time and send the invite while you're still on the phone. Run the sweep from this guide: start a new call and jump to the process section. Tell them their top leaks before you hang up, then ask once for the Field Efficiency Audit. Nothing to write up afterward: the free part stays on the call.
checklist: Lock the day and time, and send the invite now
Confirm the best number and email
Note their biggest pain so you open the sweep with it

learn_opener.question: Learning opener: ask for advice, not a meeting
say: Hi, is this {{contact|the owner}}?
My name's {{me}}. I'm starting a business helping {{trade}} with the office side of things, and I'm calling a few owners around Denver to learn how they actually run it.
Could I ask you two quick questions?
learn_opener.why: Every word is true, and people like helping someone who's learning. You're not pitching. You're collecting real stories, and the good conversations turn into shadow visits.

answers.label: Wrong person: get a name and time
Voicemail: hang up, try again in 2 days

learn_honest.question: "Are you selling something?": tell the truth
say: Fair question. Eventually, yes. I help companies fix this stuff, for a fee.
But today I'm mostly trying to learn how {{trade}} actually run things. If something you tell me sounds like a fit, I'll say so straight, and you can say no.
Fair? Two questions.
learn_honest.why: Being straight about it builds more trust than dodging. Most people relax once you've admitted it.

learn_wand.question: Question 2: the magic wand
learn_wand.say: Second one: if you could wave a wand and fix one thing about how the office side runs, what would it be?
learn_wand.why: Let them talk. If they go on about it, open Go deeper. Write their exact words in Notes.

learn_bridge.question: Thank them, then ask to see it in person
say: This is really helpful, thank you.
Honestly, the best way for me to learn is to see it. Could I come sit with you or your office for a morning and just watch how a job moves? I'll bring a notebook, not a pitch.
If I see something worth fixing, I'll tell you once, and you decide if you ever want help with it.
learn_bridge.why: A shadow visit is an easy yes, and it's the best discovery you'll get. If they're clearly in pain and asking for help, skip ahead to the audit.

answers.label: Real pain, wants help now: offer the audit
No visit, but happy to stay in touch

close_shadow.question: Book the shadow visit
say: Great. What morning works best, a busy one ideally?
Who should I sit with, you or whoever runs the office?
And what's the one thing you'd want me to make sure I see?
close_shadow.why: Ask for a busy morning, because a quiet day teaches you nothing. Watch one real job move from start to finish. You aren't selling at the visit. If something's clearly broken, mention it once at the end and offer the audit.
checklist: Lock the day and time, and send an invite
Get the address and who you'll sit with
Ask what they want you to make sure to see
Afterwards, send a short thank-you with the one thing you noticed

close.question: Bridge: summarize in their words, then confirm
say: Let me make sure I heard you right.
The big ones sound like {{pains}}.
You said that's costing you {{cost}}.
And if one thing ran itself, it'd be {{wish}}.
Did I get that right?
close.why: Play their pain back before you pitch anything. A 'yes, that's it' here makes the ask feel like the obvious next step. Use their words, not the tag labels.

answers.label: "Yeah, that's it": ask for the audit

audit_ask.question: Ask for the Field Efficiency Audit, then stop talking
say: Here's what I'd suggest. No sales meeting, no slides. I do one thing: a 90-minute Field Efficiency Audit.

I ride out to a job site with you, map how a job moves from the field to the office to a {{finishLine}}, and hand you a one-page blueprint showing exactly where your team is burning cash. I'd start with {{topPain}}.
It's a flat $750, and it comes off the build price if you have me fix it within 30 days.
I only take a couple of these a month, before the winter slowdown. The blueprint is yours either way, to use with me or without me.
Do you have a job site walk scheduled Tuesday or Thursday morning?
audit_ask.why: Offer two specific days, then let the silence sit. Their first answer is usually an objection, not a no. Handle it and ask again.

answers.label: "Need to talk to my partner / spouse"
"Can't you just tell me what to fix?"

audit_price.question: Price pushback: acknowledge, anchor to their cost, offer a smaller step
say: Fair question.
You told me {{topPain}} is costing you {{cost}}. The audit is about putting a number on that and a plan to stop it.
And if you have me build the fix within 30 days, the $750 comes off the build, so it doesn't cost you anything extra.
If it's a timing thing, let's put it on the calendar for when it makes sense.
audit_price.why: Don't drop the price, and don't trade it for free work. Tie it to the cost they already admitted. If they need time, get a date, not a discount.

answers.label: Book it for a later date
Needs to think: set a callback

audit_partner.question: "Need to check with my partner"
say: Makes total sense. Who's that?
Honestly, they should be in the room. They'll see things you don't.
Let's put a time on the calendar for the three of us. If they're not into it, you cancel with one email. Fair?
audit_partner.why: Bring the other decision-maker in instead of letting the deal wait on a conversation you're not part of.

answers.label: They'll check first, set a callback

audit_timing.question: "Busy season, maybe later"
say: Totally get it, that's when it hurts most.
When does it slow down for you?
Let's put it on the calendar for then, so the fixes are in before next season instead of during it.
audit_timing.why: Turn 'later' into a date. A future booking still counts as a booking.

audit_tip.question: "Just tell me what to fix": give one real tip, then re-ask
say: Sure, here's one you can do this week: {{tip}}
That's one fix. The audit is that, across the whole business, and in the right order.
Want to grab Tuesday or Thursday?
audit_tip.why: Giving one real piece of value builds trust. If there's no tip for their pain, give your own best quick fix.

answers.label: I'll try that first, set a callback

audit_send.question: "Send me something first"
say: Happy to, I'll send it today.
Let's pencil in a time anyway so it doesn't fall through the cracks. If what I send doesn't make sense, just reply 'cancel' and that's it.
Tuesday or Thursday?
audit_send.why: A tentative booking plus an email beats an email alone. Make cancelling easy and they're more likely to say yes.

answers.label: Just the email, follow up in 2 days

close_audit.question: Lock it in
say: Great. I'm sending the invite now. What's the best email?
One thing up front: at the end of the walk, if there's something worth fixing, we'll talk about what a build looks like. If not, no hard feelings. Fair?
And what would make that morning a win for you?
close_audit.why: Agree up front on what happens after the audit, so nobody is surprised by a pitch at the end. Ask what would make the hour a win, and write their answer in Notes. Open the report with it.
checklist: Send the invite while you're still on the phone
Who else should be there (ops manager, PM, office)?
Pick a real job site to walk, and ask them to bring their job list or spreadsheet
Write down what a win looks like for them

close_callback.question: Set a real next step
say: Totally fair. Let's not leave it as 'sometime'.
What's better, later this week or early next?
I'll send a quick invite, and next time we'll pick up on {{topPain}}.
close_callback.why: Get an exact time and agree on what you'll talk about. A calendar hold gets answered. 'Call me next week' usually doesn't.
checklist: Pin an exact day and time, and send the invite now
Confirm the best number and email
Write down which pain to lead with next time (in Notes)

close_exit.question: Polite exit
say: No problem at all, I appreciate you giving me a couple of minutes.
Out of curiosity, what would have to change for this to be worth a conversation?
Mind if I check back in a few months?
And is there anyone you know who's drowning in this stuff that I should talk to?
close_exit.why: Leave on good terms and ask for one thing: what would change their mind, permission to follow up, or a referral. Today's 'no' is often next season's 'yes'.
checklist: Note why: not a fit, bad timing, or already handled
Note what would change their mind
Got a referral? Add it to the lead sheet

guess.label: Make a guess
guess.title: Educated guesses: one at a time, then stop talking

guesses.ask: I'd bet the status of every job lives in one or two people's heads. Am I wrong?
guesses.label: Status lives in someone's head
guesses.tip: Don't ask the field to update anything. Set a 5-minute call at the same time every day (say 3:30) where the office asks three things: what moved, what's stuck, what do you need. The foreman just talks, and the office keeps the record.
guesses.fix: A job board in the app they already pay for, updated from the daily call. Jobs stuck past their usual time show on Monday's stuck list for the owner.

guesses.ask: If you added up everything owed to you right now, would you know the number?
guesses.label: Don't know money owed
guesses.tip: Turn on the automatic invoice reminders in QuickBooks or Xero. They're built in and free, and a lot of contractors never switch them on. Then add a pay-by-text link, so the customer can pay from the driveway.
guesses.fix: Automated: the invoice goes out the day the job is marked complete, reminders at 7, 14 and 30 days come from the accounting software, and a Friday money-owed report lands in the owner's inbox.

guesses.ask: When everyone's out on jobs, who answers the phone?
guesses.label: Missed calls on job days
guesses.tip: Call your own number at 2 pm on a weekday and hear what a customer gets. If it's voicemail, change the greeting to promise a text back within 15 minutes, and keep that promise.
guesses.fix: Missed-call text-back from the phone feature in their CRM, or a business phone service if it doesn't have one. The reply lands in the lead inbox with a callback task.

guesses.ask: When a quote doesn't get a reply, does anyone follow up?
guesses.label: Quotes go quiet
guesses.tip: Make the follow-up a question they can answer: "Did the price land where you expected, or should we look at options?" gets replies that "just checking in" never does.
guesses.fix: Automated: follow-up texts and emails on day 2, 5 and 10 that stop once the quote is signed, plus a weekly list of quotes about to go cold. Jobber has this built in, and most field-service tools do.

guesses.ask: When the crew does extra work on site, how does it end up on the invoice?
guesses.label: Field extras not billed
guesses.tip: Price the common extras in the contract up front, so the crew can say yes on site without calling you, and require one photo of each extra.
guesses.fix: Automated: a photo checklist for extras in the field app adds a line item to the invoice. The crew takes a photo, and nobody retypes it.

guesses.ask: How do you ask for reviews? Is it automatic, or when someone remembers?
guesses.label: Reviews not asked for consistently
guesses.tip: Ask in person at the end of the job, then text the direct write-a-review link before you leave. Use the link that opens the review form, not your Google listing.
guesses.fix: Automated: when the invoice is paid, the customer gets a review-request text with the direct link, and one reminder 3 days later.

guess.why: Read their size first. Under 30 reviews: the owner does everything, so talk about their time. 30–150: owner plus one overloaded office person, your sweet spot. 150+: managers and software, so ask for operations. Ask one guess, then stop talking. If they say yes, tag it, give the free tip, and save the fix for the audit. If you're wrong: "Oh, interesting, how do you handle that?"

paths.label: None fit: ask how they handle it
Plenty there: bridge to the close

dig.label: Go deeper ↓
say: Tell me more about that.
Can you give me a recent example?
How long has that been going on?
What have you tried so far?
Roughly what's it costing you: hours a week, jobs, dollars?
How do you feel about that?
dig.why: Use this when they mention a pain. A pain they haven't put a number on won't close, so get the cost in their own words. Ask one question at a time and let them talk.

capture.label: What it's costing them (their words)
capture.placeholder: e.g. 5 hrs a week chasing permits

paths.label: That's enough, bridge to the close

too_busy.label: Too busy
say: Totally get it. Busy is exactly when things slip, and that's who I work with.
Give me 60 seconds and one question. If it's not relevant, I'll let you go.
too_busy.why: Ask for a tiny, bounded slice of time. If they really can't, book a specific time instead.

doing_fine.label: We're doing fine
say: Good, that's honestly who I like talking to. The shops that are struggling don't have time to fix anything.
Usually 'fine' means the owner is holding it together personally.
If you took two weeks off, what would fall apart first?
doing_fine.why: Agree, then ask a question that puts them in a specific situation. 'What would fall apart' usually turns up the real pain.

wont_use.label: My guys won't use it
say: Totally, and honestly most crews won't. That's why I don't build anything that needs your guys doing data entry.
The field keeps doing what they already do: talk, text, take photos. The office captures it, and the system does the rest.
Right now, who's the one person who knows where every job stands?
wont_use.why: This is often the real objection behind 'we tried software'. Agree with it. Your rule is that the foreman is where the information comes from, not the person typing it in.

have_software.label: We already have software
say: Great, most of the folks I work with do, and most only use a slice of what they're paying for.
I'm not selling software. A lot of my work is setting up what you already pay for, and fixing the handoffs between tools where someone re-types things or a job sits waiting.
Does what you have talk to the rest of your setup?
have_software.why: Agree, then move to the gaps between tools. That's where the pain usually is.

paths.label: Ask about the gaps between tools

how_much.label: How much is it?
say: Fair question. It starts with a flat $750 Field Efficiency Audit: 90 minutes on a job site with you, and a one-page blueprint of where you're burning cash.
If you want me to build the fix, builds run $5–8k, and the $750 comes off that price if you go ahead within 30 days.
But I'd rather find out if there's anything worth fixing first. Can I ask a couple more questions?
how_much.why: Give the price straight. Dodging it kills trust. Then go back to discovery.

paths.label: Wants to think, book a callback

send_email.label: Send me an email
say: Happy to, and I'll keep it short.
So it's actually useful and not generic: what's the one thing you'd want it to answer?
And what's the best email?
send_email.why: 'Send me an email' is often a polite brush-off. Asking for the one thing turns it back into a conversation.

paths.label: Got the email, follow up in 2 days

bad_experience.label: Tried consultants before
say: Ugh, I hear that a lot. What happened?
That's why the first step is a flat $750 with a one-page report. You see exactly how I think before you spend anything real, and you keep the plan either way.
bad_experience.why: Let them vent. Listening is most of the answer. Then point out that the audit is small and capped.

not_interested.label: Not interested
say: No problem, I appreciate you being straight with me.
Can I ask: is it that things are running pretty smoothly, or just not the right time?
not_interested.why: This separates 'no need' from 'no time'. The second one is a callback.
